Regenerate them from the same runtime as base, or call out the drift separately.

DoR check #7 counts `Scenario:` lines, but the stories it reads use Portuguese Gherkin. `_TEMPLATE-STORY.md` and x-story-create/x-story-epic-full emit `Cenario:` with DADO/QUANDO/ENTÃO (story-0028-0002 itself does this). So every story produced by this toolchain gets 0 scenarios, check #7 always fails, and the verdict is always NOT_READY. Under story-0028-0006, x-dev-epic-implement blocks any story whose DoR is not READY, so this would block every story. The count needs to accept `Cenario:`/`Cenário:` as well as `Scenario:`.

Phase 4 never saves the architecture plan, implementation plan, test plan or security assessment. The subagent prompts don't tell the agents to save them either. Yet DoR checks 1 and 9 require 'File exists', and checks 2 and 3 fall back to existing `tests-story`/`security-story` files. Consequences: (a) on a first run with no pre-existing plans, checks 1 and 9 fail; (b) on the reuse path (Phase 0 jumps to Phase 5 without running agents) there is no agent output, so checks 1, 2, 3 and 9 all fail and a READY story flips to NOT_READY on an unchanged re-run; (c) x-dev-lifecycle Phase 2 treats `tests-story-*.md` as MANDATORY, and it is never produced. The story spec says the Architect, QA and Security agents generate these artifacts, and its Gherkin checks for `tests-story-XXXX-YYYY.md`.

The staleness check works against itself. The sentinel is mtime(story) <= mtime(tasks file). Phase 4.1 writes the tasks file, then Phase 4.5 rewrites the story file (Section 8.1), and Rule 5 also writes PO amendments into the story. After any successful run the story is newer than the tasks file, so every later invocation counts as stale: all 5 subagents relaunch and Section 8.1 is appended again. This breaks the RULE-002 idempotency the PR claims. Use an artifact that is written after the story update as the sentinel, such as the planning report the story spec names (its DoR Status is updated in Phase 5), or write the story update first.

The freshness marker `tasks-story-XXXX-YYYY.md` is the same file x-lib-task-decomposer writes, called from x-dev-lifecycle Phase 1C. If the lifecycle or decomposer has already run for a story, x-story-plan sees a 'fresh' tasks file and skips all planning, so no task plans and no planning report are produced and DoR fails. Only `--force` recovers. The reverse also happens: the lifecycle reuses x-story-plan's tasks file, which has a different schema. Story-0028-0002's acceptance criterion specifies the planning report as the sentinel and the log message 'Reusing existing planning artifacts'.

`total_checks = mandatory_passed + conditional_applicable` makes the denominator depend on how many checks passed. With 2 failed mandatory checks and no applicable conditionals, the report says 'Passed: 8/8' next to 'Verdict: NOT_READY'. That misleads readers and contradicts the `checks_total` contract. It should be `10 + conditional_applicable`.

Task ordering is phase-first: all RED tasks, then all GREEN, then all REFACTOR. That batches every failing test before any implementation, which breaks the per-cycle Red-Green-Refactor TDD the project requires and the interleaved RED/GREEN/REFACTOR sequence in `_TEMPLATE-TASK-BREAKDOWN.md`. The SKILL.md algorithm also drops the planning guide's rule that a dependency comes before its dependents. As a result, tasks such as SEC RED tasks that depend on ARCH GREEN tasks get lower TASK-NNN numbers than their prerequisites.

The MERGE key is only 'same component + same layer' and ignores `tdd_phase` and the test scenario. A QA RED task (components [UserValidator, UserValidatorTest]), the QA GREEN task and the ARCH GREEN task for UserValidator in the domain layer all match and collapse into one task with conflicting TDD phases, wiping out the RED/GREEN pairing and TPP sequence. MERGE also runs before AUGMENT and absorbs any SEC task on the same component, which contradicts AUGMENT's 'Do NOT remove the original SEC task'. Even the guide's examples (ARCH+SEC merged vs ARCH+SEC augmented) are resolved differently, so the result is not deterministic.

PAIR only checks QA-NNN GREEN tasks. The Architect is told to mark every implementation task GREEN (line 248), and SEC also emits GREEN tasks. Any of these that were not merged end up as production-code tasks with no failing test before them, which violates test-first. It also contradicts planning-guide.md line 117: 'Every GREEN task MUST have exactly one RED predecessor'.

The implementation map path is `plans/epic-XXXX/IMPLEMENTATION-MAP.md`, but x-story-map (listed as the upstream skill) and x-story-epic-full save it as `plans/epic-XXXX/implementation-map-XXXX.md` (e.g. `plans/epic-0028/implementation-map-0028.md`). Phase 1.3 will always log 'Implementation map not found' and plan without dependency context.

The story-file update has several problems. (1) `_TEMPLATE-STORY.md` already contains '## 8. Sub-tarefas' with an '### 8.1 Detailed Tasks (Multi-Agent Planning)' placeholder table, but the skill writes a new '## 8. Sub-Tasks' / '### 8.1 ...' block 'below it'. That produces duplicate 8.1 sections, and since every run counts as stale, one more is appended each run. (2) The skill's columns (#, TDD Phase, Depends On, Effort) don't match the template's (Agent, DoD, Status). The Status column is what story-0028-0004 uses to mark TASK-NNN complete. On re-runs the existing 8.1 should be replaced, not appended.

Required story updates are missing. Story-0028-0002 says the story Status must change to 'Pronta para Desenvolvimento' when READY (and stay 'Pendente' otherwise), and that Section 4 DoR checkmarks must be updated. Phase 5 only updates the planning report, so the `story_status_update` output in the data contract is never produced.

'Language: English ONLY' conflicts with epic RULE-006, which story-0028-0002 lists as applicable: all content generated by planning skills must be pt-BR, except technical terms and IDs. The sibling planning skills (x-story-create, x-story-epic, x-story-map, x-story-epic-full) use the pt-BR policy, so this skill's planning reports, task plans and amended Gherkin will be in the wrong language.

Conditional checks 11 and 12 look for a compliance assessment with regulatory mapping in the Security agent's output, and for contract-test scenarios in the QA agent's output. Neither prompt asks for these: Security only reads the compliance KP (lines 307-308), and QA never mentions contract tests. In compliance- or contract-enabled projects these checks will usually fail, making the story NOT_READY.

The new core skill is picked up automatically by SkillsAssembler.selectCoreSkills, so every profile's generated output gains `skills/x-story-plan/**`. GoldenFileTest's completeness check (extra files) will therefore fail for all 17 profiles, and the `claude-skills`/`codex-skills` counts in smoke/expected-artifacts.json go out of date. These run under failsafe, which is why the 5521 surefire tests still pass. The story DoD also requires at least one automated test validating the SKILL.md frontmatter and required sections, and none is added. Deferring this to story-0028-0007 means merging a red `mvn verify`.

The implicit 'Domain layer tasks before application layer tasks' and 'Application before adapter' edges are added between every pair of tasks in those layers, regardless of type. Combined with explicit dependencies, they can create spurious cycles. Example: a domain-layer SEC test task that depends on the adapter task it augments (as the Security prompt instructs) becomes a cycle with the implicit domain→adapter edge. Step 3 then aborts the whole run with 'Circular dependency detected'.

TPP order is inconsistent. The QA prompt orders levels nil → constant → scalar → conditional → collection → iteration, while consolidation (line 494) and planning-guide.md line 194 order them ... → collection → conditional → .... TPP and the story template both put conditions before iterations/collections, so consolidation reorders the QA agent's test sequence incorrectly, and DoR check 2 checks against yet another numbering.

No agent is ever asked to produce REFACTOR tasks. QA emits only RED+GREEN pairs, ARCH only GREEN, SEC RED/GREEN, TL/PO VERIFY. Yet the ordering (line 489) and DAG (line 504) assume REFACTOR tasks exist, the story spec has QA proposing RED/GREEN/REFACTOR, and the project rules require explicit refactoring after green.

Check #10 requires the planning report to exist 'with all sections populated', but its DoR Status section is only filled after validation (line 795). Read strictly, the check fails against the skill's own output, or the result depends on interpretation.

The inline task-breakdown table doesn't match `_TEMPLATE-TASK-BREAKDOWN.md`. It omits Test Scenario Ref, Tier and Budget, uses TASK-001 where the template uses TASK-1, and says Agent/DoD are 'extended from standard template' when the template already has them. The DoR inline format (Mandatory/Conditional sections) also differs from `_TEMPLATE-DOR-CHECKLIST.md` (Architecture/Test/Security... Readiness). So output differs depending on whether templates are present, contrary to the claim that the inline format produces 'the same conceptual sections'. Downstream consumers of the tasks file (x-dev-lifecycle, x-lib-task-decomposer reuse) expect the template schema.

The TASK_PROPOSAL schema departs from the story's data contract. The contract specifies source enum ARCHITECT/QA/..., type DEV/TEST/SEC/QUALITY/VALIDATION and effort as 'Nh'; the skill uses XS–XL T-shirt sizes, which can't be summed into the 'Estimated Effort {total}' field. Section 3.1 also lists an `implementation` type that isn't in the enum. The merged-task source is `merged(a,b)`, but the acceptance criterion expects Agent = "MERGED".

Phase 0 runs `mkdir -p` (0.2) and the mtime staleness comparison (0.3) before checking that the story file exists (0.4). A missing story can therefore create stray `plans/epic-9999/plans` directories, and if an old tasks file exists the comparison runs against a nonexistent file before the 'Story file not found' abort. The existence check should come first.

`allowed-tools` omits `Agent`, even though Phase 2's core purpose is dispatching 5 subagents. Other subagent-dispatching skills in this repo list it (x-codebase-audit, x-threat-model, x-hardening-eval). The story contract also specifies `AskUserQuestion` and an argument-hint that accepts a story path; neither is reflected here.

The change updates only one golden copy (java-quarkus/.claude x-dev-lifecycle). GoldenFileTest checks byte-for-byte parity for all 17 profiles. These goldens still have the old content: x-dev-lifecycle in the other 16 profiles' .claude dirs, the .agents/.codex copies (about 70 files hold this skill), and every golden copy of x-dev-epic-implement and x-dev-implement. `profile_whenCalled_matchesGoldenFiles` will fail for every profile, so the PR's claim that 'All existing tests pass' cannot hold. Regenerate the goldens before merging.

The DoR pre-check is never wired into the real flow. The Core Loop in Section 1.3 (lines 621-625) still goes straight to `updateStoryStatus(IN_PROGRESS)`, and the default parallel dispatch (1.4a steps 1-3) marks every executable story IN_PROGRESS and launches them all in one message with no DoR step. The snippet places the check in step 6, which runs after steps 4/5 have already dispatched the stories. In default (parallel) mode, NOT_READY stories will still be implemented. Do the check before partitioning and dispatch (e.g., filter in step 1/3 or in getExecutableStories), and update 1.3 and 1.4a themselves rather than a copy inside 1.1b.

The verdict lookup doesn't match what x-story-plan writes. A `## Final Verdict` section exists only in `_TEMPLATE-DOR-CHECKLIST.md`, and there it is free text (`{{VERDICT_DETAIL}}`). The inline fallback in x-story-plan Phase 5.3 has no Final Verdict section; the verdict is in the Header table and in `Verdict: **READY**` (bold). An exact `verdict == READY` check on that section will often find nothing. The case where the file exists but the verdict is missing or unrecognized is not covered, and `{failed_checks}` has no defined source (Blockers vs 'Blockers and Open Questions'). Define a robust extraction (Header `Verdict` row, then the `Verdict:` line) and a fallback for an unparseable verdict.

A story BLOCKED by DoR stays blocked forever. It gets no `blockedBy`, and Resume Step 2 keeps BLOCKED when `blockedBy` is undefined. The DoR check never runs again on `--resume`, even after the user re-runs x-story-plan and gets READY. Its dependents get no block propagation (that only fires for FAILED) and stay PENDING, so the epic never reaches a terminal state for them. Also, `reason` is not a StoryEntry field (use `summary`). Re-evaluate the DoR on resume and propagate the block to dependents.

The path template `dor-story-{storyId}.md` (and `tasks-story-{storyId}.md` at line 539) breaks when storyId is the checkpoint/StoryEntry id (`story-0042-0001`, as in the JSON example and schema). That gives `dor-story-story-0042-0001.md`, which never exists. A missing file is treated as 'proceed (backward compatible)', so this mismatch silently turns the whole DoR gate off. Spell out the path explicitly (`dor-story-XXXX-YYYY.md` / `dor-{storyId}.md`).

Task-level resume keeps DONE tasks and claims the subagent 'receives the task state and skips DONE tasks automatically'. Nothing implements that: the dispatch prompt in 1.4 is unchanged and RULE-001 passes metadata only. It is also unsafe. A story that is resumed or retried (IN_PROGRESS/FAILED → PENDING, old PR closed) gets a fresh lifecycle run that creates `feat/{STORY_ID}-…` from develop, often in a new worktree. The commits of 'DONE' tasks are not on that branch, so skipping them ships an incomplete story. Reset task state when the story restarts on a new branch, or pass the existing branch and task state to the subagent explicitly.

Per-task status is written only in Phase 8, after all tasks, PR creation and reviews, and only as DONE. Nothing initializes the `tasks` map (agent/type). Nothing writes IN_PROGRESS or DONE per task during Phase 2, and `commitSha`/`duration` are never recorded although the schema marks them required when DONE. If a story is interrupted, which is the only case per-task resume exists for, `tasks` is absent or empty, so Step 1b and the per-task checkpoint in x-dev-epic-implement do nothing. Update task status after each task commit in Phase 2.

The lifecycle subagent now writes `execution-state.json` directly. In the default parallel mode each lifecycle runs in an isolated worktree (`isolation: "worktree"`), so it writes a copy the orchestrator never reads, or several subagents race on the same file. Elsewhere the checkpoint is owned by the orchestrator via `updateStoryStatus` and written atomically (1.6). When the lifecycle runs standalone there is no execution-state.json at all. Return task results in SubagentResult and let the orchestrator persist them.

PRE_PLANNED can effectively never be reached. It needs all 7 artifact types, and lists architecture/tests/plan/security/compliance as produced by 'x-story-plan Phase 2A/2B/2C'. x-story-plan has no such phases and writes only tasks-story, task-plan-TASK-*, planning-report and dor-story; the DoR checks were just changed to read the planning report instead of standalone files. `compliance-story` is also only produced when compliance is active (1F is conditional). Stories planned by x-story-plan/x-epic-plan will always come out HYBRID, so task-by-task execution and per-task checkpoints never activate.

The freshness rule `mtime(story) <= mtime(artifact)` is defeated by the workflow itself. x-story-plan Phase 4.5 rewrites the story file (Section 8.1 and PO amendments) after it writes the tasks file and task plans. The epic orchestrator's markdown sync also rewrites the story Status (Em Andamento) around dispatch. The story is therefore always newer than the tasks/task-plan artifacts, so they look stale. The same applies to x-dev-implement's 'are fresh' requirement for Task-Aware mode. A stale tasks file also gets regenerated by the Phase 0 pre-check/x-lib-task-decomposer, which overwrites the multi-agent breakdown and leaves the task-plan files out of sync.

The mode table has gaps. If all artifacts exist but some are stale, PRE_PLANNED fails, HYBRID ('some exist but not all') doesn't match, and INLINE ('none exist') doesn't match, so no mode applies. HYBRID also says to reuse existing 'fresh' ones without saying what happens to existing stale ones. Define the fallthrough explicitly (e.g., HYBRID = regenerate missing or stale artifacts).

The new 'Phase 0.5 — Planning Mode Detection' reuses the number of the existing 'Phase 0.5 — API-First Contract Generation' right below it, at a different heading level. The Workflow Overview is not updated either. Two different Phase 0.5s make phase references and progress messages ambiguous. Rename it (e.g., a Phase 0 step).

The PRE_PLANNED Phase 2 path drops the quality gates of the standard flow: no `{{COMPILE_COMMAND}}` between tasks, and no `{{TEST_COMMAND}}`/`{{COVERAGE_COMMAND}}` with the 95%/90% thresholds, only 'acceptance tests pass'. It also commits every task as `feat(...)`, including RED test-only tasks (Conventional Commits wants `test:`). VERIFY tasks (TL/PO/retained SEC) produce no changes, so an 'atomic commit' for them fails or is meaningless.

The resume check treats a task as DONE when its file/class exists and that component's tests pass. That is true before any work for every task that modifies an existing class. It is always true for REFACTOR tasks, whose precondition is passing tests. So on a normal first run these tasks are skipped silently and logged as 'resume point verified'. Base resume on recorded task state or commit history (e.g., a TASK-NNN commit on the branch), not on file existence.

'Tasks with no deps before those that have deps, then TDD phase, then TPP level' is not a topological order. With a chain A→B→C, B and C both 'have deps', and the secondary keys can put C before B. The tasks file already has an explicit dependency DAG. Require a topological sort, using phase/TPP only as tie-breakers.

Every task is committed as `feat(scope): implement TASK-NNN [TDD:GREEN]`, whatever its phase. RED (test-only), REFACTOR and VERIFY tasks get a GREEN tag, which falsifies the TDD history that lifecycle Phase 8 and x-review-pr check ('commits show test-first pattern'). It also contradicts the lifecycle's `[TDD:RED|GREEN|REFACTOR]`. The compile check runs after the commit, so non-compiling code can be committed. Validating the DoD also doesn't stop the commit when it fails.

Per-task plans (`task-plan-TASK-*`) are produced by x-story-plan, not by x-dev-lifecycle (line 89). Lines 390/396 say `x-lib-task-decomposer`, which only writes the tasks breakdown, so the attribution is wrong there too. It also writes the same `tasks-story-*.md` filename in a different format, so detection can mix a decomposer breakdown with x-story-plan task plans. The 'Mode A'/'Mode B' names used in step 5 are not defined anywhere in this skill.

`EPIC_DIR` resolution is applied only partly. Phase 0.5 still checks `plans/epic-XXXX/story-XXXX-YYYY.md`, so a suffix-variant epic dir (`plans/epic-XXXX-*`) aborts with 'Story file not found'. Phase 1.4, the Phase 4 outputs (lines 536-702) and the final artifact list still hardcode `plans/epic-XXXX/plans/`, while `mkdir -p <EPIC_DIR>/plans` creates a different directory. Downstream consumers (x-dev-lifecycle, x-dev-epic-implement, x-epic-plan) also hardcode `plans/epic-XXXX/`. Multiple suffix matches with no exact match are not handled.

Renumbering TPP Level 4 to collection and Level 5 to conditional makes x-story-plan disagree with x-test-plan (Level 4 = Complex Conditions, Level 5 = Iterations). DoR check #2 still validates 'TPP level ordering (1 through 6)' and accepts the x-test-plan `tests-story` file as fallback evidence. The same numeric level now means different things in the two skills.

Retained SEC tasks are forced to `tdd_phase: VERIFY` and ordered after the implementation they verify. The Security subagent is still told (line 343) to emit RED tasks for security tests. A security test written as RED becomes a post-implementation check, which loses test-first for security behavior and contradicts the RED/GREEN pairing rule.

The per-task schema doesn't match its producers or the rest of the file. The `type` examples (DEV/TEST/SEC/REFACTOR) are not x-story-plan task types (architecture/implementation/test/security/quality-gate/validation). `agent` cannot represent merged sources like `merged(Architect,Security Engineer)`. Task `duration` is in milliseconds while story `duration` is in seconds. There is no dependencies field, which Step 1b needs to unblock BLOCKED tasks, and a dependency that is SKIPPED never counts as satisfied.

The hook checks the wrong checkout. It runs inside the team lead's session, the one calling SendMessage, so `git symbolic-ref HEAD` and `process.cwd()/.dev-team/.reviews` both point at the lead's own checkout. The implementer's branch and worktree are never looked at. The task skill and agent-teams-guide put implementers in `isolation: "worktree"` on their own branches while the lead stays on main. In that normal setup line 91 always sees `main` and allows the shutdown, so the guard never blocks anything. If the lead is on a different branch (`develop`, `trunk`, or some feature branch), the guard checks that branch's sidecars instead of the implementer's and blocks for no good reason. The header comment's claim that it checks for 'open, unreviewed PRs' is also wrong: no PR or implementer branch is ever resolved. To fix this, work out the target agent's branch, for example from the task list, the assessment, or a recorded agent→branch mapping, and look for sidecars in that worktree.

Review evidence is detected only by finding the sanitized branch name inside a sidecar's filename. Under ADR-029, review-gate writes sidecars as `<agent>--<contentHash>.json`, so the branch name never appears in the filename. Real review sidecars will therefore never match, and once the hook gets this far it blocks every implementer shutdown even after reviews ran. That trains users to add `--force-shutdown` by habit. merge-gate already solves this by reading the sidecar's `branch` JSON field and using the filename only as a fallback, plus lstat/symlink filtering; this hook should share that logic. The substring match is also loose: `feat-12` matches `feat-123-...`, so a sibling branch's sidecar can satisfy the check.

Shutdown is allowed as soon as any sidecar exists. Reviewers write sidecars when they produce findings, which is before anything is routed to or acknowledged by the implementer. So the exact failure this hook targets is still allowed: the implementer gets shut down after review but before routing, possibly with unresolved `[DEFECT]` findings. The README entry ('Blocks shutdown ... before review findings are routed') and the task skill's requirement to stay alive until findings are acknowledged both say more than the hook enforces. At minimum, apply the same check as review-gate Gate 2 and block while any non-LIGHT sidecar has a `[DEFECT]` finding without `resolved: true`.

`workflow.review` is typed as `WorkflowToggle = boolean | "complex"` (src/init.ts), but the hook only special-cases `=== false`. With `review: "complex"`, SIMPLE tasks are presumably not reviewed, yet the guard treats every implementer as needing review evidence and blocks its shutdown. The hook should read the branch's assessment sidecar (`.dev-team/.assessments/<branch>.json`, ADR-043) and enforce only for COMPLEX branches when the setting is `"complex"`.

For string messages, shutdown is detected with `message.includes("shutdown_request")`. Any ordinary message to an implementer that mentions the word (e.g. 'don't expect a shutdown_request until review is done') is treated as a shutdown and can be blocked. Only the structured `{type: "shutdown_request"}` form should count. Separately, the block message says 'Use --force-shutdown' without saying where to put it in a structured message. It only works because the whole object is stringified, so it has to go in a free-text field such as `reason`.

The 'allows shutdown with review evidence' test uses a made-up sidecar name, `knuth--feat-123-test.json`. Real sidecars follow the ADR-029 `<agent>--<contentHash>.json` format, so this test passes while real usage would always block. The suite also runs with the hook's cwd set to the implementer's branch, which builds in the wrong assumption that the lead and the implementer share a checkout. Tests that would catch these problems are missing: a realistically named sidecar with a `branch` field, a lead on main shutting down an implementer on a feature branch, a string message mentioning shutdown_request without `--force-shutdown`, and `workflow.review: "complex"`. The `extraEnv` parameter of `runGuard` is never used.

Every non-wrapper binary fails its probe because of a quoting bug. The heredoc uses an unquoted delimiter (`<<SH`), and in that kind of heredoc `\"` is not an escape, so the backslashes stay in the generated script: `binary_path="$(command -v \"jq\" || true)"`. A `$(...)` inside double quotes is parsed separately from the outer quotes, so `\"` becomes a literal quote and the shell runs `command -v '"jq"'`. That lookup always fails, the probe prints `missing_binary:jq` and exits 1. Check 3 will therefore always fail on the first manifest entry (jq), and so will the sandbox check, before gemini is ever reached. `bash -n` can't catch this. The base version used a quoted heredoc, so `"${binary}"` was correct there. Fix: use `command -v ${binary}` (or `'${binary}'`), or pass the binary and smoke command as positional args to `sh -c` instead of interpolating them.

If the quoting bug above is fixed, this loop silently stops after the first entry. It reads entries from a here-string (`done <<< "${entries_json}"`), and every iteration calls `gce_ssh`, i.e. `gcloud compute ssh`. Without `-n`, ssh reads its stdin to EOF and forwards it to the remote side, even when the remote command never reads it. The first SSH call therefore consumes all remaining manifest lines, the next `read` hits EOF, and the loop exits. Only the first entry (jq) gets verified. Gemini, the binary this PR is about, and every other binary are skipped while verify reports success: the check fails open. The old code made a single SSH call, so this is new. Fix: give each in-loop `gce_ssh` stdin from `/dev/null` (or pass `--ssh-flag=-n`), or read the loop from a different file descriptor (`while read -r entry_json <&3; ... done 3<<<...`).

The verifier now takes its list of required binaries from the runner's checkout (`scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json`) instead of from the manifest baked into the deployed image. The in-image manifest is only checked for existence (`test -f`); its contents are ignored. `verify.yml` checks out the workflow ref, not `DEPLOYED_REF`. `deploy-staging-on-release.yml` runs on `workflow_run`, so the checkout is the default branch HEAD rather than `workflow_run.head_sha`, and a manual production verify runs against whichever branch it was dispatched from. Whenever the checkout and the image differ (commits landed after the release, rollbacks, production verified from dev), verify either fails falsely on binaries the image never promised, or misses checking binaries the image's own manifest lists. Fix: read the in-image manifest (e.g. `docker exec ... cat` or `docker run --entrypoint cat`) and parse it locally with jq, or check out `DEPLOYED_REF`.

`runtime_wrapper_bin` now comes from `OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN` in the CI runner's environment. Before, it was read inside the container, where the Dockerfile sets it. `verify.yml` never sets it, so the path is hard-coded to `/opt/daisy/bin`. If the image ever changes its wrapper prefix, verify will look in the wrong place, and an unrelated runner env var could also redirect the check. Read the value from the target, e.g. `docker exec <c> printenv OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN` or `docker image inspect` for the image.

Splitting the single probe into per-entry remote calls takes one SSH session per check, previously one per target. Each target now needs about 14 IAP-tunneled `gcloud compute ssh` sessions: the manifest check, the arch check, one per non-wrapper binary, and two for the wrapper. That is roughly 28 per run when sandboxing is on, and in image mode each one also starts a fresh `docker run --rm` container. This adds minutes to verify and gives IAP/SSH flakiness many more chances to cause spurious failures. Only wrapper-backed entries needed direct exec. Non-wrapper entries could still go through one batched shell probe per target.

Any non-zero exit from `gce_ssh` is reported as "Runtime binary manifest missing". That includes transport failures: IAP tunnel errors, ssh exit 255, `docker exec` failing because the container is gone. Operators will be pointed at image provisioning when the real problem is connectivity, the same verifier-vs-image confusion this PR set out to fix. The same applies to the wrapper `test -x` check at 267-268. Distinguish exit 1 from `test` from other failures, or word the message to cover both.

The `image` branch of `build_target_direct_exec_command` copies the smoke-suffix parsing, the metacharacter guard, and the arg re-quoting from `build_direct_exec_smoke_command` instead of calling it. It could pass `sudo docker run --rm --entrypoint <path> <image>` as the prefix, though that would require separating where the binary path and args go. The `smoke_suffix`, `arg` and `smoke_args` locals are also unused in the container branch. If the two copies drift, container and sandbox verification will behave differently. Also, the guard's `*'\\'*` pattern matches two consecutive backslashes, not one. This is harmless only because `printf '%q'` re-quotes every arg anyway.

`getHtml` returns `quill.root.innerHTML`, which is Quill 2's internal editor markup, not portable HTML. Quill 2 renders every list as `<ol>` and tells bullets apart only by `data-list="bullet"`. It marks indents with `ql-indent-N` classes and wraps code blocks in `<div class="ql-code-block">`. The server-side HtmlSanitizer strips `data-*` and `class` attributes by default, and recipients don't have Quill's CSS. So every bullet list arrives as a numbered list, and indentation and code-block formatting are lost. Rich→Markdown has the same problem: Turndown turns bullet lists into `1.` lists and code blocks into plain text. Use `quill.getSemanticHTML()` (Quill 2 API), which produces proper `<ul>`/`<ol>`/`<pre>` markup.

`setHtml` assigns `quill.root.innerHTML` directly, which skips Quill's clipboard matchers and Delta model. marked emits tags Quill doesn't model (`
    `, `
    `, tables, raw HTML), so after switching Markdown→Rich, the DOM and Quill's internal content can disagree. `isEmpty()`/`getText()` and undo history then become unreliable, and the content isn't normalized. marked also passes raw HTML through, so markdown such as `` runs when injected via innerHTML (self-XSS). Use `quill.clipboard.dangerouslyPasteHTML(html)` or `setContents(quill.clipboard.convert({ html }))`, ideally after sanitizing the marked output.

`ImapClient.GetFolder(SpecialFolder.Sent)` doesn't return null when the server lacks SPECIAL-USE/XLIST; it throws `NotSupportedException`. So the `?? GetFoldersAsync(...)` fallback only runs on servers that support SPECIAL-USE but have no \Sent folder. On servers without the extension, including GreenMail used in dev, the outer catch swallows the exception and the copy is never saved to Sent. No Sent folder is created when missing, the name match only covers "Sent" (not "Sent Items" or "Sent Messages"), and `PersonalNamespaces[0]` can throw when the list is empty. Check `client.Capabilities` before calling `GetFolder`, fall back to name matching, and create the folder if it doesn't exist.

Only `InvalidOperationException` is caught, and it is always turned into 404 "Mailbox not found". SMTP failures (SmtpCommandException, AuthenticationException, SslHandshakeException, SocketException, CryptographicException from Unprotect, MimeKit ParseException) escape as raw 500s. The `SendMailFailed` resource added in this PR is never used. Several MailKit exceptions also derive from `InvalidOperationException` (`ServiceNotAuthenticatedException`, `ServiceNotConnectedException`). For example, when `SmtpRequiresAuth` is true but no password is stored, MailSendingService.cs:76 silently skips auth, the server replies 530, MailKit throws ServiceNotAuthenticatedException, and the user sees "Mailbox not found". Use a dedicated not-found result or exception type, and map send failures to a localized error (e.g. 502 or 400 with `SendMailFailed`).

`ConnectAsync(host, port, bool useSsl)` maps `true` to implicit TLS (SslOnConnect) and `false` to opportunistic `StartTlsWhenAvailable`. The mailbox form and entity default to port 587 with SmtpUseTls=true, which means an implicit-TLS handshake on the STARTTLS submission port. That fails with SslHandshakeException for most providers. MailTestEndpoints uses explicit `SslOnConnect`/`None` instead, so the connection test and the real send disagree. With TLS unchecked, the test connects in plaintext but send tries STARTTLS and can fail on self-signed NAS certificates. Pass an explicit `SecureSocketOptions` that matches the test endpoint, e.g. SslOnConnect for 465 and StartTls otherwise.

The CC/BCC toggle only hides the inputs; it doesn't clear them. Addresses typed in and then collapsed are still parsed, validated and sent, so hidden BCC/CC recipients get the mail even though the user may believe they removed them. Validation errors for cc/bcc render only inside the collapsed block, so an invalid hidden address makes Send silently do nothing. Either clear the values when collapsing, or keep the section open whenever it has values or errors.

Minimal APIs don't enforce DataAnnotations here: there is no `AddValidation()` or manual validation. `[Required]`, `[MinLength(1)]`, `[MaxLength(1_048_576)]`, `[StringLength(998)]` and the ContentType regex have no effect. A request with a missing `to` causes a NullReferenceException at ComposeEndpoints.cs:26. A null `subject`, or a null `body` with plain content type, throws ArgumentNullException in MimeKit. All of these surface as 500s, and body size is only bounded by Kestrel's 30 MB default. Validate explicitly in the endpoint or enable built-in validation.

The server's error body is read into `error` and then discarded, and a generic "Failed to send" is always shown. The API returns specific localized messages (invalid address with the offending email, mailbox not found) that the user never sees. Parse and display `message` from the response.

HTML mail is sent as a single `text/html` part with no `text/plain` alternative. This hurts deliverability (spam scoring), plain-text-only clients and accessibility, and `TextBody` is null for the stored copy. Use MimeKit's `BodyBuilder` with both `HtmlBody` and a plain-text rendering, which gives multipart/alternative.

The Message-Id comes from the parameterless `MimeMessage()` constructor, which calls `MimeUtils.GenerateMessageId()` with the local machine/container hostname as the domain. That leaks the internal host name and often produces a non-FQDN id, which spam filters penalize. Generate it from the sender's domain, e.g. `MimeUtils.GenerateMessageId(MailboxAddress.Parse(mailbox.EmailAddress).Domain)`.

The '404 for invalid mailbox' test stubs `IMailSendingService` to throw, so the mailbox ownership check the PR advertises is never tested. No test has one user try to send through another user's mailbox. MailSendingService has no tests for MIME building, sanitization, or Sent-folder behavior. `SendMail_WithCcAndBcc_CallsServiceAsync` uses `Arg.Any<SendMailRequest>()`, so it doesn't verify that CC/BCC reach the service.

`postCreateCommand` installs `.[dev]`, but `pyproject.toml` has no `[project.optional-dependencies]` and the build backend is hatchling. Hatchling ignores the `extras_require` in `setup.py`, so the `dev` extra does not exist. uv only prints "does not have an extra named `dev`" and still exits successfully. As a result pytest, pytest-asyncio, mypy, black, ruff and types-requests never get installed in the container, and the README's `pytest` / `mypy .` / `black .` / `ruff .` commands fail. Define a `dev` extra or dependency group in pyproject.toml, or install from `requirements-dev.in`. The README line saying 'installs all Python dependencies automatically' (README.md:65) is wrong for the same reason.

`workspaceFolder` is hard-coded to `/workspaces/ProxmoxMCP-Plus` and `workspaceMount` is not overridden. The source is still bind-mounted at the default `/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}`. If the clone directory has any other name (a fork or worktree, a different name passed to `git clone`, or a lowercase name, since Linux paths are case-sensitive), VS Code opens a directory that does not exist, `postCreateCommand` fails because its cwd is missing, and the interpreter path at line 20 points nowhere. Remove `workspaceFolder` and use `${containerWorkspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python` for the interpreter.

This turns on `editor.formatOnSave` with Black as the default Python formatter, but the codebase is not Black-formatted: it uses single quotes and has lines well over 88 characters, e.g. `src/proxmox_mcp/config/loader.py:64-84`. Because black is not installed in the venv (missing `dev` extra), the extension falls back to its bundled Black, which is newer than the `black<24` pinned in setup.py/requirements-dev.in. Every save reformats the whole file, so contributors' PRs fill up with unrelated formatting changes. Drop formatOnSave, or reformat the repo once and pin the formatter version first.

`uv venv` creates `.venv` in the bind-mounted workspace, the same path the README's host install tells contributors to use. If a contributor already has a host `.venv` (macOS/Windows), `uv venv` replaces it with a Linux venv, or warns/errors depending on the uv version, which is unpinned. That breaks the host environment. Switching back to a host venv then breaks the container's interpreter. Put the container venv somewhere else (e.g. `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` / `VIRTUAL_ENV` outside the workspace, or a named volume mounted over `.venv`).

`--no-install-recommends` on top of `python:3.11-slim` leaves git without its recommended `openssh-client` and `less`. With an SSH remote (`git@github.com:...`), `git fetch` and `git push` fail inside the container with `cannot run ssh`, even though Dev Containers forwards the host SSH agent. Without `less`, git's pager is missing. Install `openssh-client` (and `less`) explicitly.

The build context is `..` (the whole repo), but the Dockerfile copies nothing, and the repo has no `.dockerignore`. Every image build sends `.git`, `.venv` and `proxmox-config/config.json` (which contains Proxmox API token secrets) to the Docker daemon for no reason. Use `"context": "."` or drop the context.

`PROXMOX_MCP_CONFIG` is never set (no `containerEnv`/`remoteEnv`), unlike the production Dockerfile. After following README step 3, running `python -m proxmox_mcp.server` (the README's Development Mode) silently ignores `proxmox-config/config.json` and falls back to env vars, so it fails with 'Proxmox host must be provided'. Set `PROXMOX_MCP_CONFIG` to `${containerWorkspaceFolder}/proxmox-config/config.json`.

This step implies the OpenAPI proxy is reachable at http://localhost:8811 once the container is up, but nothing starts it. The user still has to run `./start_openapi.sh`. In browser-based Codespaces the forwarded port is served from a `*.app.github.dev` URL, not localhost. Document the start command and the Codespaces URL behaviour.

Nothing deploys this new topics file. Every other topics file under nais/topics has its own .github/workflows/deploy-*-topics.yml that calls reusable-topic-workflow.yml (for example deploy-aktivitetspenger-soknad-topics.yml), but this PR adds no such workflow. So the three dusseldorf.aktivitetspenger-inntektsrapportering-* topics are never created in Aiven dev or prod. Once deployed, KafkaProducerService will fail to produce to the mottatt topic and the endpoint will return 500 (MeldingRegistreringFeiletException). The three new Kafka Streams will also go to ERROR because their source topics are missing. Add a deploy-aktivitetspenger-inntektsrapportering-topics.yml workflow.

AKTIVITETSPENGER_INNTEKTRAPPORTERING journals with the placeholder brevkode "FIXME_AVP_INNTEKT_BREVKODE". The new endpoint has no feature toggle, so real income reports will be archived in dokarkiv under an invalid brevkode. Classification and routing downstream depend on the brevkode, and journalposts that are already created cannot be fixed afterwards. Get a real brevkode before merging, or gate the endpoint until there is one.

The income report is encoded as a plain Aktivitetspenger k9 søknad, with søknadsperiode set to the reporting month and the default søknad validator (AktivitetspengerSøknadValidator). Nothing in it marks it as a report. The ungdomsytelse equivalent sets UngSøknadstype.RAPPORTERING_SØKNAD and no søknadsperiode. Here the k9 payload looks like a real aktivitetspenger application for that month; the only difference is that `inntekter` is non-null. A consumer that reads the k9 format (ung-sak, or a fordel based on the journalpost JSON) could treat an income report as a new application. Agree on an explicit type marker in the k9 contract, or leave out søknadsperiode, before this goes live.

These ACLs differ from both sibling topic files, which looks unintentional. aktivitetspenger-soknad-mottatt and ungdomsytelse-inntektsrapportering-mottatt both grant read to k9saksbehandling/ung-brukerdialog-api, and so do both siblings' cleanup topics. The new mottatt and cleanup topics do not; the cleanup topic grants only ung-sak (lines 63-69). If ung-brukerdialog-api consumes these topics the way it does for the other flows, its consumers will be denied. Check which consumers need access and align the ACLs.

`@AssertTrue fun harOppgittInntekt()` never runs. Hibernate Validator only treats get*/is*/has* methods as bean properties, and "har" is none of those, so this is just an unenforced return-value constraint during bean validation. A request without arbeidstakerOgFrilansInntekt passes @Valid, and a null income is sent to the k9 format and to RapportertInntektDto, despite the message "Må ha oppgitt inntekt". The same applies to OppgittInntektForPeriode.harOppgittInntekt (OppgittInntektForPeriode.kt:15-17). Rename the method to e.g. `isOppgittInntekt`/`hasOppgittInntekt`, or use `@field:NotNull`. If null is meant to be allowed, remove the misleading constraint.

The oppgave is marked as løst only after the message has been produced to Kafka and the duplicate-check key has been set. If markerOppgaveSomLøst fails (it rethrows after retries), the user gets an error even though the report has already been sent for journalføring. A retry within the dedup TTL is then rejected as a duplicate, and the oppgave stays open in ung-brukerdialog-api. The ungdomsytelse flow has the same pattern, but it is worth handling here: catch and log or alert instead of failing the request, or reconcile asynchronously.

The aktivitetspenger controller test imports the ungdomsytelse fixture (no.nav.brukerdialog.ytelse.ungdomsytelse.utils.InntektrapporteringUtils), so it posts an UngdomsytelseInntektsrapportering. It only passes because the two JSON shapes happen to match today, and it will hide regressions if the aktivitetspenger model diverges. Import no.nav.brukerdialog.ytelse.aktivitetspenger.utils.InntektrapporteringUtils instead.

PDF_PREFIX = "ung" and the ids "1-full-inntekt-alle"/"2-arbeidstaker-og-frilansinntekt" are the same as in UngdomsytelseInntektsrapporteringPdfGeneratorTest. The two tests write to the same files and overwrite each other's readable output, which can also race when tests run in parallel. Use a distinct prefix such as "aktivitetspenger-inntekt".

Editing a source URL silently deletes its stored token. When the URL changes, the UI moves the mask to the new key (`{[newUrl]: '*'}`) and removes the old key, expecting the backend to carry the token over. The comment here says the same ("transferred from a renamed one"). But the `"*"` case only looks up `existingCred.Env[u]` under the new URL, which never exists. The old URL is also no longer active, so its token is dropped. If no other tokens remain, the whole credential is deleted. Changing the branch or adding `.git` to a private-repo URL therefore loses the PAT, and later syncs fail with auth errors. If you add a transfer, keep it on the same host (or require the token to be re-entered). Otherwise an admin could send a stored token they can't read to a host they control just by renaming the URL.

Backward-compatibility regression. Before this change, `GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN` was used for every github.com catalog URL, for both the clone and the API size check. Now it is used only when the URL exactly matches a hard-coded `https://github.com/obot-platform/mcp-catalog`. Deployments that sync private GitHub repos through `GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN`, or that point `OBOT_SERVER_DEFAULT_MCPCATALOG_PATH` at their own fork, will stop syncing after upgrade. Every other GitHub source now hits api.github.com unauthenticated (60 requests/hour per IP); chart/values.yaml says this token exists to avoid exactly that rate limit. The stated reason (not leaking the token to attacker-controlled endpoints) doesn't apply: the old code only sent it to github.com. Keep the fallback for any github.com host, and compare against the configured `defaultCatalogPath`, not a constant.

Scheme-less inputs are now rewritten in `SourceURLs` (`github.com/org/repo` becomes `https://github.com/org/repo`), but the keys of `SourceURLCredentials` are not. The UI keys the token by the raw text the user typed. The check at L169-172 then finds that key isn't an active URL and skips it, so the PAT is silently discarded. The URL is saved without a token, and the sync of the private repo fails. Apply the same normalization to the credential keys, or reject keys that don't match.

`isGitRepoURL` now treats every gitlab.com URL as a git repository. Raw-file sources on gitlab.com used to be fetched as plain files and worked, e.g. `https://gitlab.com/org/repo/-/raw/main/catalog.yaml` or `/api/v4/projects/.../raw` URLs. They now go through `parseGitURL`, which reads `-/raw/main/...` as a branch name and rejects it because it starts with `-`. Existing catalogs using these URLs break on upgrade. Consider classifying gitlab.com URLs that contain `/-/` or `/api/` as raw files.

The clone now uses `osfs.New(tempDir)` instead of `git.PlainClone`. `osfs.New` defaults to the legacy ChrootOS filesystem, which follows symlinks during checkout. As far as I know, go-git's `PlainInit`/`PlainClone` have used `osfs.WithBoundOS()` since v5.11, which keeps resolved paths inside the base directory. With this PR, arbitrary third-party hosts can be cloned, so losing that guard against a crafted repo or server writing through a symlink outside the temp dir weakens security. Use `osfs.New(tempDir, osfs.WithBoundOS())`.

The catalog spec is saved before the credential is written. If `CreateCredential` or `DeleteCredential` fails, the API returns an error but the new URL is already saved without its token. When the admin retries "Add", it fails with "duplicate URL found". Separately, if the last sync was more than an hour ago, the spec update can start a sync that reads the credential before it has been stored. Write or delete the credential first, then update the catalog.

`sizeLimitedFS` wraps both the `.git` storer and the worktree, so the 100 MB budget is shared by the compressed packfile, the index, and the uncompressed checkout. A repo with roughly a 50 MB pack whose files expand to 50+ MB will be rejected as "repository is too large (limit: 100 MB)". That makes the real limit about half the advertised one, and inconsistent with the GitHub and GitLab API checks, which measure repo size. Consider counting only the packfile writes, or document the effective limit. (Lines refer to the wiring in pkg/controller/handlers/mcpcatalog/github.go.)

List and Get now reveal the plaintext credential just to compute a presence mask, and they return an error on any credential-store failure other than not-found. A temporary credential-store problem therefore breaks the whole catalog listing and the admin MCP Servers page, even though the masks aren't needed to render it. Consider logging the error and leaving `sourceURLCredentials` out instead.

The comment says credential-store failures will be "visible in the sync status", but they are only logged. The sync then continues with an empty token, so the admin sees a misleading "authentication required" or 404 error for the private repo instead of the real cause. The credential is also re-revealed once per source URL. Reveal it once per sync and record any failure in `SyncErrors`.

The doc comment for `readGitCatalog` ("clones a git repository over HTTPS...") was merged into the comment above `parseGitURL`, so `parseGitURL`'s doc now describes the wrong function and `readGitCatalog` (L277) has none. Move the first two lines down to `readGitCatalog`.

The output directory is built from `skillset.name`, which comes from the untrusted remote manifest (validateSkillset only checks that it is a string). A name like `../../../../../../home/victim` sends tmpDir outside the temp area. safePath can't catch this because it only checks paths against tmpDir, which has already escaped. Together with manifest file entries like `../../.bashrc` (which normalize to `.bashrc` and are fetched from attacker-controlled raw.githubusercontent URLs), a malicious skillset can overwrite arbitrary user files such as ~/.bashrc and get code execution. Validate or sanitize the name (e.g. a strict slug regex, or reject path separators and `..`), and check every write against a fixed, trusted root.

The branch segment of `https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/<branch>/path` is matched but thrown away. SkillIdentifier has no ref field, and resolveIdentifier always uses the repo's default branch. A URL for `tree/develop/...`, a tag (`tree/v1.0.0`) or a commit SHA quietly installs content from the default branch instead: wrong files, version pinning ignored, and possibly a confusing 404 if the path only exists on that branch. The new test 'parses GitHub URL with non-main branch' passes only because it doesn't check the branch. Carry the ref through to ResolvedLocation and skip the default-branch lookup when a ref is given.

safePath uses `resolved.startsWith(baseDir)` with no path separator, so sibling directories with the same prefix pass. With baseDir `/tmp/spm/fsd`, an entry path that normalizes to `../fsd-evil/x` resolves to `/tmp/spm/fsd-evil/x` and is accepted. Use `path.relative(baseDir, resolved)` and reject results that start with `..` or are absolute, or compare against `baseDir + path.sep`.

Files go to a predictable shared path, `os.tmpdir()/spm/<name>`. On Linux that is the world-writable /tmp, so another local user can create `/tmp/spm/<name>` (or symlinks inside it) first. mkdir with recursive:true and writeFile both follow existing symlinks, so the victim's install can be redirected to overwrite their own files, or end up with attacker-planted content alongside the downloads. Use a per-run `mkdtemp` directory or a project-local directory. This also contradicts the PR description, which says files are stored in `.tmp/<skillset-name>/`.

Every entry is downloaded with `location.ref`, the main skillset repo's default branch, including cross-repo `@owner/repo/path` skill sources. If the other repo's default branch is different (e.g. `master`), or a non-default ref was intended, those downloads 404 or fetch the wrong content. Each foreign repo needs its own ref, either from its default branch or from an explicit ref in the source.

The new `..` check only covers bare-path sources. `./` relative sources (e.g. `./../../x`), `@` cross-repo paths, `files` entries, `setup`, and the agents/hooks/mcp/memory/rules lists all build paths from manifest data with no traversal check, so the protection is inconsistent and gives a false sense of safety. The substring check also rejects legitimate names such as `skills..v2`. Validate path segments (reject any segment equal to `..`) once, for every manifest-derived path.

All downloads are read with `response.text()` and written back with 'utf-8' (install.ts:86, and the same pattern in download-from-url.ts and read-local-file.ts). Skills can ship binary assets such as images, PDFs, fonts or archives, and these get silently corrupted by UTF-8 decoding and re-encoding. Download as ArrayBuffer/Buffer and write the bytes unchanged.

The GitHub URL regex captures everything after the branch as the path, including a trailing slash, query string or fragment. Pasting a URL like `.../tree/main/claude/fsd/` or `...?tab=readme` produces a manifest path such as `claude/fsd//skillset.yml` or `claude/fsd?tab=readme/skillset.yml`, which won't resolve. Branch names that contain `/` (e.g. `feature/x`) are also mis-split into the path. Parse with `new URL()` and strip trailing slashes.

Writes are keyed only by the repo-relative `result.path`, so entries from different repos (cross-repo skills) with the same path collide. They are written concurrently to the same file and the last one wins. Also, the target directory is never cleared between runs, so files from an earlier install of the same skillset stay mixed in with the new download.

Every file is fetched at once with an unbounded Promise.all. For large skillsets this can trip raw.githubusercontent.com rate limits or exhaust sockets, and the first failure rejects everything with no retry. Consider a small concurrency limit.

This test passes even though the command fails: `test-skillset` is rejected by parseIdentifier and the process exits with code 1, and neither the exit code nor stderr is checked. It also runs readConfig against the git root, which writes `.spmrc.yml` into the repo; that is likely how the stray `.spmrc.yml` ended up committed. Nothing tests the new install flow itself (safePath, ref handling, writing files).

This looks like an artifact auto-created by readConfig when running `spm install` or the integration test from the repo root. It isn't mentioned in the PR and shouldn't be committed; either remove it or gitignore it.

`vi.restoreAllMocks()` does not undo `vi.stubGlobal`; that needs `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` or the `unstubGlobals` config. The stubbed fetch therefore leaks past the test's cleanup. The same pattern is in download-from-github.test.ts and download-from-url.test.ts. The `mkdtempSync` temp directories created at module level are also never removed.

The new Deployment is missing the `envFrom: secretRef: ms-secret-vault` block. The shared Helm chart added this to every service (charts/templates/deployment.yaml:76-78). Without it, none of the Vault-backed secrets reach the pod. The mounted config (backend/ai-secure-agent-config.yaml) sets MySQL user `root` with no password, so the password and any LLM/API keys come only from that secret. The agent will start without credentials and fail to authenticate to MySQL and other dependencies. Add `envFrom: - secretRef: name: ms-secret-vault`.

`agent-app` tracks the feature branch `AI-20-AISecureAgent-Feature-collection`. Every other Application and the ApplicationSet track `HEAD`. Once this merges, the `agent/` manifests on main are not what Argo deploys, so later edits on main are silently ignored. If that branch lacks `agent/` or is deleted after merge (the usual practice), the app goes into ComparisonError. Because `prune: true` is set, a diverged branch can also remove resources. Point it at `HEAD` (or main).

The migration drops the liveness and readiness probes that the Helm values defined (`/ai-secure-agent-ms/v1/ping`). Without a readiness probe, the Service sends traffic to the pod before the app (MLflow init, Kafka/MySQL connections) is ready. Without a liveness probe, a hung Python process is never restarted. Port the probes over.

The resource requests and limits from the Helm values (100m/256Mi requests, 200m/345Mi limits) are gone, so the pod is now BestEffort with unbounded memory on a shared k3s node. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` is still set, which suggests memory growth was a known problem for this workload. An unbounded agent can starve or OOM-evict the other microservices. Restore the requests and limits.

Cutover risk: deleting helm_backend/ai-secure-agent-ms makes the `helm-app` ApplicationSet delete the generated `ai-secure-agent-ms` Application. ApplicationSet-generated apps carry the resources finalizer by default, so that deletion cascades to resources with the same names this new app creates (Deployment `ai-secure-agent-ms`, Service `ai-secure-agent-ms-svc` in `default`). Depending on ordering, both apps claim the same resources (SharedResourceWarning, tracking label flip-flopping), or the old app's cascade deletes the live Deployment and Service and causes downtime until `agent-app` re-syncs. Plan the handover explicitly, e.g. set `preserveResourcesOnDeletion` or remove the finalizer first, or sync `agent-app` after the old app is gone.

The image is now a hard-coded `repo:tag` string in a raw manifest instead of `image.tag` in helm_backend/<svc>/values.yaml. The release automation (see commits like `chore(<svc>): bump tag to ... [skip ci]`) updates the values.yaml path. Without an update, new ai-secure-agent builds will not be deployed, or the bot will recreate helm_backend/ai-secure-agent-ms/values.yaml, which makes the ApplicationSet generate a second, conflicting app again. The `isBase64` heuristic in `decodeSecretKey` corrupts valid credentials. client-go already returns decoded `Secret.Data` bytes, and the operator writes these secrets single-encoded (`create_admin_secret`). So any username or password that happens to fit the base64 alphabet, with a length divisible by 4, gets 'decoded' a second time into random bytes. The operator generates 16-character passwords from a 70-character alphabet (`ascii_letters + digits + '!@#$%^&*'`). About 14% of those, (62/70)^16, use only alphanumerics and are silently mangled, so authentication fails with a 401 that is hard to diagnose. User-supplied values like `Password1234` or usernames like `root`/`user` are hit the same way. Remove the double-decode and return `string(raw)` as-is.

In cluster mode the server URL comes from `status.endpoints.admin`. The operator always sets that to `http://{name}-keycloak.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:8080` (`keycloak_reconciler.py:464-467`), and `public` gets the same value. This CLI runs on a workstation or CI host, which cannot resolve cluster-internal DNS. AGENTS.md calls out exactly this failure for integration tests. The code comment says it prefers admin because the toolkit runs outside the cluster, but admin is the internal URL. As a result the default, documented flow (every cluster-mode example in the docs and help text leaves out `--server-url`) fails with a DNS or connection error. Possible fixes: derive the URL from `spec.ingress.host`/`tlsEnabled`, open a port-forward, or require `--server-url` and say so in the docs.

The fallback builds a URL from `spec.hostname` and `spec.tls.enabled`, but the Keycloak CRD has no `spec.hostname`. The hostname fields are `spec.ingress.host` and `spec.tls.hostname`. Also, `status.endpoints.internal` is never set by the operator. So these fallbacks are dead code, and the error message points users to a field that doesn't exist. `internal/k8s/types.go` models the same non-existent field.

The response parsing doesn't match Keycloak's `PartialImportResults`. That object has `added`, `skipped`, `overwritten` and `results[]`, and each result's `action` is ADDED, SKIPPED or OVERWRITTEN. There is no `errors` count and no ERROR/FAILED action. This means: (1) the advertised 'hard fail on errors > 0' (lines 90-96) is dead code, because real failures come back as non-2xx responses with the whole request rolled back; (2) `overwritten` is never read, so `--mode overwrite` reports Added: 0, Skipped: 0 even when every user was replaced. Parse `overwritten` and drop the fictional error accounting. Also add an `httptest`-based test against a real response shape.

The ADR rests on a wrong premise. Keycloak runs each `partialImport` request in a single transaction and calls `setRollbackOnly` on any error, so a batch is atomic. Partial progress only happens across batches. The 'errors > 0 in SKIP mode' agent instruction refers to a response field that doesn't exist. These statements will mislead future agents and maintainers. The same claim appears in the `--batch-size` row of `docs/how-to/migration-toolkit.md:259` ('Partial Import is non-atomic').

The only way to pass the explicit admin password is the `--password` flag, which puts the master-realm admin password in process argv. Other local users and monitoring agents can read it via `ps` or `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, and shell history may record it. The documented CI pattern `--password "$KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD"` still expands into argv. Support an environment variable such as `KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, a `--password-file`, or `--password-stdin`, and recommend that in the docs instead.

Authentication, token refresh, HTTP and transport failures all return a `nil` result. `runImportUsers` then calls `printImportSummary(nil)`, which prints nothing, so the 'Print partial result before returning error so user can see progress' path never runs for the most common failures. After batch 7 of 10 fails, the user cannot see how many users were already added. Return the accumulated `result` together with the error.

`http.DefaultClient` has no timeout, here and at line 174. A stalled Keycloak or a load balancer that drops the connection makes the migration hang forever mid-batch. Use a dedicated `http.Client` with a sensible or configurable timeout. There is also no way to supply a CA bundle for Keycloak instances behind an internal CA.

Every 409 is labelled `(mode=FAIL)`. Partial Import also returns 409 for any `ModelDuplicateException`, which can happen in SKIP or OVERWRITE mode, for example a conflicting unique constraint such as a federated identity link. The hard-coded label sends the user in the wrong direction. Report the actual mode that was used.

`--batch-size 0` or a negative value is silently changed to 500 instead of being rejected. Validate it in the command, and also guard `chunk()`: called directly with `n <= 0` it loops forever, because `i += 0` never advances.

If both `--keycloak` and `--username`/`--password` are given, explicit credentials silently win and `--keycloak` and `--namespace` are ignored. The docs say 'Exactly one mode must be chosen'. Either reject the combination or fix the docs.
Only `Ready` is accepted. The project's phase semantics (AGENTS.md / TESTING.md) treat `Degraded` as operational too, so a running Keycloak in `Degraded` blocks the import and there is no override.

This reads the user-supplied `spec.admin.existingSecret` rather than the operator-managed `{name}-admin-credentials` copy, which is always kept in sync and recorded in `status.adminSecret`. The operator itself always reads the copy. Reading the original needs extra RBAC on a secret that may be managed elsewhere, and it ignores the legacy `spec.admin_access` alias. It also contradicts the PR description, which says the command reads the operator-generated secret.

The 'stale export' check uses the mtime of `users.json`. That measures time since `transform` ran, or since the last `cp`/`git checkout`, not how old the export is. The error's advice to re-run `transform` just resets the mtime on the same stale data. The check gives a false sense of safety, and the 24h default will block the multi-day GitOps rollout in the docs' own Full Migration example. Also, `%.0f hours` prints '0 hours' for sub-hour limits.

Only `chunk()` and the loader are tested. Nothing covers `authenticate`, `importBatch`, token refresh, `ImportUsers` error paths, `decodeSecretKey`, `resolveURL`, `ResolveFromFlags`, or `parseImportMode`. Both high-severity bugs above, credential mangling and the internal-DNS URL, plus the wrong response schema, would have been caught by simple `httptest` and table tests. The 85% patch-coverage requirement is not plausibly met for this code.

The default path requires `get` on Secrets in the Keycloak namespace and gives master-realm superadmin credentials to whoever runs the CLI. That conflicts with the project's core 'least privilege: no access to the Keycloak instance other than through the CRDs' requirement. The ADR presents both paths as 'equally valid' and never records this deviation or its trade-off.

This pins client-go/apimachinery v0.32.3, which pulls in `golang.org/x/net v0.30.0` and `golang.org/x/oauth2 v0.23.0`. The module already targets Go 1.25, so use a current k8s.io release.
